DISCUSSION
Hydraulic and pneumatic systems have several characteristics in common but also are completely different.

The hydraulic system uses hydraulic fluid to transfer energy from the pump through the system to perform work and then returns the fluid to a reservoir for reuse. Hydraulic fluid does not compress and the pump runs continuously with a pressure bypass circuit to keep the hydraulic fluid moving through the pump for lubrication and cooling.....

Air and other gases can be compressed. In a pneumatic system the pump operates to compress the air into the receiver, or storage tank, and then shuts down. The pressure in the system is used as needed and then exhausted to the atmosphere. The pump heat is dissipated using cooling fins and an internal oil reservoir provides lubrication.....

While many of the component parts in hydraulic and pneumatic systems perform the same function and have the same name, almost none of the parts are interchangeable. The hydraulic fluid properties are much different than the properties of air under pressure...

Liquid hydraulic fluid cannot be compressed. The pressure applied by the hydraulic pump cannot be stored and must be bled through a bypass valve when not used by hydraulic system to perform work. The system accumulator often maintains an even pressure by utilizing a bladder of compressed gas or a spring-driven piston..........................

Gases, such as air, can be pressurized. The pressurization bleeds off as the air is used by the system equipment and the pump is cycled to keep the pressure in the system between two levels. Pressure is maintained by a storage tank, the receiver, which is primarily an empty sealed container...
While different in application, the problems which develop in both systems are almost the same. Both systems experience similar failures and can be troubleshot in similar manners:

Both the typical hydraulic or pneumatic systems have many components. Components are attached throughout the system using couplings and a series of pipes, tubes, and hoses. Leaks in both systems reduce the system functionality and can be dangerous to the operator and others in the area.n the area...

Leaks can occur in both the suction and the discharge side of the pump. Leaks in the suction side of a pneumatic pump can allow dusty or contaminated air into the system. This could lead to pump failure, component binding, and clogged lines...

Leaks in the suction side of a hydraulic pump allows air into the system. This could lead to pump cavitation, "water hammers", contamination, corrosion, dangerous equipment movement, and premature failures...
DEFINITION

WATER HAMMER - The result of a sudden change in liquid velocity. Liquid is not compressible and any energy that is applied to it is instantly felt throughout the system. This energy becomes dynamic in nature when a force such as pump cavitation pulses velocity to the fluid...

Tests for leaks at the intake of a hydraulic system can be done using an eyedropper or syringe. Apply small amounts of hydraulic fluid to all joints and seams in the suction circuit and pump housing with the pump running. The leak will draw the fluid into the system at the faulty joint...

Leaks on the suction side of a pneumatic system using air as the fluid medium are usually due to a damaged or missing air cleaner at the intake. Never allow operation of a pneumatic system without a working air filter...

Leaks in the system on the pressure side can usually be spotted or heard. Hydraulic fluid in an uncommon area or puddles of fluid in an unusual area are signs of leaking, cracked, or broken hoses, plumbing, or junctions...

Listening for leaks is the best way to diagnose pneumatic leaks in the system, the hissing sound is unmistakable. Always keep your hands away from any suspected leaks to avoid personal injury. Use a foreign object to confirm the leak...
Always remember to power down and tag the system prior to performing any maintenance. Any residual pressure should also be bled off prior to attempting repairs.

Air in a hydraulic system and moisture in a pneumatic system greatly affects system performance. greatly affects system performance.

Should the fluid level become low in a hydraulic reservoir a vortex or whirlpool may form in the fluid and air can be pulled into the suction side of the pump. Air can also enter the system through loose fittings, cracks, and bad gaskets on the suction side...

Air can enter fittings on the pressure side when the hydraulic system is powered down. But, you can expect the fitting allowing the air leak with no pressure to also seep fluid when under pressure. After repair the system must be bleed to purge the air...

The opposite of air in a hydraulic system is water in a pneumatic system. Moisture accumulates in a pneumatic system on a routine basis due to the heating of the air that occurs during compression and the condensation that can happen when the air is cooling..

A receiver that fills with air quickly or compressors that cycle on and off often are indicators of a receiver with too much water accumulation. The moisture should be drained from the system on a regular basis, daily on large industrial systems. Moisture drains are provided on all receivers and most aftercoolers and air line filters.....
Pneumatic systems with excessive internal moisture will operate erratically. Too much moisture can also increase corrosion and rust in the system.

The output of a pneumatic piston pump is a gas under pressure, usually air. Lubrication is provided by an onboard supply of oil kept away from the output pressure. Cooling is provided by cooling fins on small-to-medium systems and automotive-type liquid cooling systems on larger systems...

Piston pumps have fewer parts to wear out that will cause slippage. The piston rings and the valves are the only parts which normally wear and are usually replaced during repair or rebuilding that have a direct effect upon the pressure. Gaskets are always replaced when any teardown is performed...

Other parts, such as bearings and gaskets may fail and have an affect on the output pressure. But the cost of rebuilding a worn piston pump are minimal when compared to other pumps discussed in this lesson...
Actuators can also experience slippage resulting in erratic operation and creeping when set in one position.
DEFINITION
CREEP - To shift gradually out of place.here.
Fluid or air can slip past the packing, piston rings, or o-rings during operation causing incomplete motion and loss of power.
Creeping occurs in application like hydraulic actuator cylinders on fork lifts. The actuator will not hold position and slowly returns to the rest position as the pressure bleeds off.

Rebuilding an actuator cylinder usually requires the replacement of the piston rings, packing, or o-rings, and the replacement of packing material or seals at rod ends.

Rotary actuators are usually maintenance free except for leaks at the shaft seals. Some rotary actuators in high pressure applications use sliding vanes which can have additional wear at the vane/casing sealing point...

The check valve in this application prevents fluid from flowing back into the reservoir after the equipment is shut down. This shortens the initial fluid flow time and extends the pump life as the fluid does not prime all the way from the reservoir...

Should the check valve wear to the point slippage occurs the pump must work longer upon initial startup before fluid starts flowing in the system as the pump primes from the reservoir. Pump life may also be shortened. If the reservoir is distant from the pump the start time may be excessive...

The relief valve allows pressure to be channeled back to the reservoir when the 4-way valve is not activated. This redirection of fluid keeps fluid flow though the pump maintained at all times, keeping the pump cooler and lubricated...

A relief valve stuck closed may prevent fluid flow back to the reservoir, overheating the pump when the actuator is not in use. This may also reduce the fluid viscosity and cause increased wear in all moving parts...

Should the relief valve stick in the open position or have internal slippage the available pressure to the 4-way valve/actuator will be reduced and performance may be hampered. The flow pressure with the 4-way valve open will be lower than normal with a stuck open or slipping relief valve...

A 4-way valve with internal slippage may allow fluid to flow between the chambers and back to the reservoir. Pressure is diminished and the actuator may not move fully in both directions. 4-way valves with internal leaks and slipping may also allow the actuator to creep with the valve in the at rest position.....
